for (theta in c(0.25, 0.30)) {
  mu_fixed <- roc_pivot(mu_explainer, protected = compas_data$ethnicity,
                         privileged = "Caucasian", cutoff = 0.5, theta = theta)
  prob_fixed <- 1 - mu_fixed$y_hat
  pred_class <- ifelse(prob_fixed > 0.5, "yes", "no")
  # Accuracy = mean(pred_class == compas_data$Two_yr_Recidivism)
  # Demographic parity = prop_parity(..., probs = "prob_fixed", ...)
  # TPR gap            = equal_odds(..., probs = "prob_fixed", ...)
  # Predictive rate parity = pred_rate_parity(..., probs = "prob_fixed", ...)
}
(c) Model answer: the lecture’s pattern continues, and in the same direction, at both new theta values. Demographic parity and the TPR gap keep moving further below 1 (0.23 → 0.16 → 0.10 and 0.30 → 0.22 → 0.15), meaning the correction is not settling toward parity but overshooting further into reversed disparity. Predictive rate parity keeps getting worse (1.73 → 1.79 → 1.98), now further from 1 than the original, uncorrected model’s demographic parity gap was. Accuracy keeps falling, reaching 50.4% at theta = 0.30, which is essentially indistinguishable from a coin flip on this roughly balanced-outcome dataset. There is no point on this sweep where all three metrics look good together, but a defensible practical stopping point is around theta ≈ 0.10–0.15: this is where demographic parity and the TPR gap are closest to (without having already overshot far past) 1, while accuracy has not yet collapsed toward chance. Grading note: full credit for correctly extending the direction of every metric with real numbers. A student who explicitly notices that theta = 0.30’s accuracy is close to random guessing, and treats that as a natural stopping point, should receive credit for going beyond the minimum. Do not require the student to name the exact same “stopping point” theta as this guide, since that is a judgement call, not a fact to reproduce.


Question 6 — Why no theta satisfies every criterion
What a strong answer needs: the student must connect this specifically to differing base rates between groups, not just restate “fairness criteria conflict” as an unexplained fact.
Model answer: demographic parity, the TPR gap, and predictive rate parity can all sit at 1 simultaneously only in a special case, when the two groups’ true base rates of the outcome (here, actual two-year recidivism) are equal, or when the classifier predicts perfectly. COMPAS’s two ethnicity groups have base recidivism rates of 39.1% and 52.3%. They are not equal, and the classifier is not perfect. Demographic parity ignores the true outcome entirely, so it fully absorbs this base-rate gap in addition to any model unfairness. Predictive rate parity conditions on the prediction, which partially (but not fully) absorbs the same gap. roc_pivot’s theta can shift how much of the gap is reflected in each metric, but it cannot make the underlying base-rate difference disappear. Moving one metric toward 1 necessarily moves at least one other away from it. Grading note: a student who cites Chapter 2’s Kleinberg/Chouldechova impossibility result by name should receive full credit even without deriving it from base rates explicitly, provided they correctly state that unequal base rates (or imperfect prediction) is the condition that triggers the impossibility.

title: INSTRUCTOR SOLUTIONS — Assignment: Explainability Principles
text:
Note



Sample solutions. These are released after marking to help you review your own answers. They illustrate one strong way to answer each question, not the only acceptable one — see each question’s “what a strong answer needs” note for the standard your answer was assessed against.



How to use this guide
Most of this assignment lets students pick their own domain (insurance, lending, hiring, healthcare, or another). There is no single fixed narrative to grade against. The model answers below use insurance underwriting and pricing as the illustrative domain where a domain choice is needed, consistent with the lecture’s own worked examples, but a well-reasoned answer set in lending, hiring, or healthcare should be graded on the same criteria: correct mechanics, genuine (not manufactured) reasoning, and internal consistency with the domain the student chose. Questions 3, 4, and 5 have real, checkable technical content — grade those for accuracy, not just effort.


Question 1 — Why explainability, and when not
What a strong answer needs: in 1a, two genuinely different situations (not the same scenario relabelled), with a reasoned account of why the low-stakes case differs, not just an assertion that it’s “low stakes.” In 1b, a domain other than public-benefits administration, and a concrete account of who specifically is left unable to get an explanation and what harm follows, not a generic restatement of the lecture’s example.
Model answer (1a), insurance underwriting and pricing:

High-stakes: a claims-denial decision. It directly and often irreversibly affects the policyholder’s finances, is legally consequential (the policyholder may appeal or litigate), and can conceal discrimination against a protected group if the reasoning is never surfaced. Explainability here is not optional.
Lower-stakes: an internal fraud-scoring model that only reorders an investigator’s queue and does not itself deny or delay any claim payment. What makes this different: (i) no direct consumer-facing action follows automatically, a human investigator still reviews the flagged claim, so a false positive costs at most some investigator time, not a denied payment; (ii) publishing which behavioural signals trigger investigation would let fraudulent claimants learn to avoid detection, directly undermining the tool’s purpose.

Grading note: accept other domain-appropriate pairs (e.g., a loan-approval decision vs. an internal lead-scoring model that only orders which applicants a human reviews first), provided the reasoning engages with why the low-stakes case differs (no direct consequential action, and/or a gaming risk from disclosure), not just an assertion that it is lower-stakes.
Model answer (1b), hiring screening: an automated resume-screening tool silently downweights candidates whose resumes contain a term correlated with a protected characteristic (a real-world analogue: Amazon’s internal resume-screening tool, scrapped in 2018 after it was found to systematically downgrade resumes containing the word “women’s,” a pattern nobody inside the company could explain or catch until an internal investigation was launched). If no one, not the rejected candidate, not an HR compliance reviewer, not an external auditor, can get a checkable account of why specific candidates were filtered out, the harm compounds over time: candidates never learn why they were rejected and cannot contest it, the discriminatory pattern goes undetected because there is no local explanation to sanity-check, and by the time it surfaces (often via external investigation, as in the real case) the company has already made years of biased hiring decisions and faces reputational and legal exposure.
Grading note: the answer must name a specific party who cannot get an explanation and a specific downstream harm, mirroring the two-part structure of the lecture’s own example (a family that cannot contest, versus an oversight body that cannot review). A generic “AI can be biased in hiring too” without this structure has not engaged with the question.


Question 2 — Stakeholder mapping
What a strong answer needs: three stakeholders with a specific scope (global/local) and method matched to a stated need, not just a method name, and a 2b answer that identifies a genuine structural reason one method cannot serve all three, not merely “they have different needs.”
Model answer (2a), stakeholders = policyholder, regulator, internal model validator:








Stakeholder
Scope / method
Justification




Policyholder
Local, SHAP waterfall summarised to 2–3 drivers in plain language
Wants a contrastive answer to “why is my premium what it is,” not a population-level summary; needs plain language, not technical output


Regulator
Global, PFI (or PDP) plus a fairness cross-check
Needs to verify that no non-legitimate or proxy variable dominates model behaviour across the whole book, and that variable effects are stable where actuarially expected, a population-level audit, not one policy


Internal model validator (actuary signing off)
Global, PDP/ALE + global SHAP summary
Needs to sanity-check that the model’s learned effects across the full range of each rating factor match actuarial expectations before sign-off, which a single local explanation cannot provide



Model answer (2b): A single method cannot serve all three because the stakeholders differ on two independent axes at once: scope (global vs local) and audience sophistication (technical vs plain-language). A method built to give an exact, game-theoretic decomposition of one customer’s premium (local SHAP) does not, by itself, produce the statistical, group-level evidence a regulator needs to confirm no proxy variable is systematically inflating prices for a protected group, that requires aggregating or re-running the method globally. Conversely, a global PDP that reassures the actuary the age effect is sensible on average says nothing to an individual customer about their premium. Grading note: reject “they just want different things” without naming the two axes (scope and audience), that is the specific mechanism the question is testing.


Question 3 — Permutation Feature Importance
What a strong answer needs: in 3a, a concrete account of what a PFI ranking actually reveals (both which legitimate factors dominate and whether a non-legitimate or proxy variable contributes more than expected), and a reason it is a good first diagnostic (cheap, model-agnostic, no retraining) rather than just “it’s useful.” In 3b, a genuine pair of correlated predictors in the chosen domain and a correct account of why permuting one in isolation produces a misleading score, not just an assertion that correlation “causes problems.”
Model answer (3a), insurance underwriting and pricing: a PFI ranking run on a newly-fitted pricing model tells the validator, in one pass and without retraining, both which legitimate rating factors the model actually relies on (e.g., Age and Bonus, the no-claims discount level, ranking highest) and whether a non-legitimate or proxy variable (e.g., a constructed InsuranceScore feature) contributes more than domain knowledge would predict, an early signal that fairness scrutiny is needed before the model goes further into review. It is often the first diagnostic run because it is cheap (no retraining, just repeated scoring on shuffled data), model-agnostic (it works the same way whether the underlying model is a GLM or XGBoost), and compresses the whole model into a single ranked list that surfaces gross problems, a badly out-of-place proxy variable, or a legitimate factor contributing far less than expected, a possible data-quality issue, before more expensive local or global diagnostics are run.
Grading note: an answer that only says “PFI shows which features matter” without engaging with both the legitimate-factor check and the proxy-detection use has only partially answered the question.
Model answer (3b): in motor insurance underwriting, vehicle value and vehicle age are strongly correlated, older vehicles are typically worth less. Permuting vehicle value in isolation, while leaving vehicle age at its original values, creates combinations that essentially never occur in practice (e.g., a newly-registered vehicle now paired with a low permuted value, or a 15-year-old vehicle paired with a high permuted value). The model, scored on these unrealistic combinations, responds in ways driven by its behaviour in a region it was never trained to handle well, rather than by how much it genuinely relies on vehicle value for realistic cases. Because the two variables are correlated, the model can also partly reconstruct the permuted feature’s signal from its correlated partner, which is left untouched, understating the permuted feature’s true importance. Either way, the resulting score does not cleanly reflect the model’s real reliance on vehicle value.
Grading note: the answer must correctly identify that the problem is the unrealistic, out-of-distribution combinations created by permuting a correlated feature in isolation, not just “the variables are related so it’s confusing.” A strong answer engages with the direction of the distortion (the score can be inflated or deflated) rather than only asserting “the score is wrong.”


Question 4 — PDP’s weaknesses, and why they matter
What a strong answer needs: in 4a, correct identification of both weaknesses (feature independence and heterogeneous-effect averaging) and a correct account of how the adversarial framework exploits each, not just a restatement of the limitations in isolation from the attack. In 4b, a genuine subgroup-heterogeneity scenario, outside insurance, where the effect’s direction or magnitude actually differs across subgroups (not just “results vary a bit”), and a correct account of how overlaying ICE curves would reveal it.
Model answer (4a): PDP’s extrapolation weakness (it assumes the feature of interest is independent of the others, and can be evaluated at combinations rarely or never seen in real data) and its averaging weakness (it can mask effects that differ across subgroups or point in opposite directions) are what Xin, Hooker and Huang’s (2025) adversarial framework exploits. Their adversarial framework leaves the model’s predictions untouched on the real, densely-observed region of the data, exactly where most policyholders or applicants actually sit, but substitutes a separately chosen, non-discriminatory output only for the sparse extrapolation region that PDP’s averaging step depends on. Because that region is rarely or never observed in practice, almost none of the model’s real-world predictions change, yet the resulting PD plot for a protected or proxy variable can be engineered to look flat, exploiting exactly the fact that a PDP is a single averaged curve rather than a distribution of individual effects. In other words, the attack does not need to fix the model’s actual behaviour, it only needs to control what the model does in the region the averaging step relies on to draw the curve.
Grading note: a strong answer names both weaknesses specifically (not just “PDP has limitations”) and explains that the attack targets the extrapolation region specifically, not the model everywhere. An answer that says only “PDP can be gamed” without explaining the mechanism has not met the bar.
Model answer (4b): In hiring screening, suppose a model includes “years since last role change” as a feature. For newly-hired candidates, the feature has essentially no relationship to the score, since the whole cohort recently started a role; for tenured internal candidates being scored for promotion, the same feature has a strong positive relationship with the predicted score (longer time in a stable role reads as reliability). A PDP for this feature, averaged across the whole applicant pool, could show a weak, muddled, close-to-flat curve, because the strong positive effect in one subgroup and the near-zero effect in the other partially cancel out in the average, hiding that the feature matters a great deal, just only for one subgroup. Overlaying ICE curves for individual applicants would reveal this immediately: a bundle of near-flat curves for new-candidate profiles sitting alongside a bundle of steeply-rising curves for tenured-candidate profiles, two visibly different shapes that the single averaged PDP line disguises.
Grading note: reject an answer that only asserts “results vary across observations” without specifying what varies (direction, magnitude) and for which subgroup or observed characteristic.


Question 5 — Choosing between SHAP and LIME
What a strong answer needs: a 5a recommendation grounded in SHAP’s actual guarantees (local accuracy, consistency), not a vague preference, and a 5b risk scenario grounded in the mechanics of LIME’s instability (kernel width, sampling randomness), not just “LIME is less reliable.”
Model answer (5a): Recommend SHAP (TreeSHAP, if the model is tree-based). Two of its properties matter directly here. Local accuracy (\sum_j \phi_j = \hat f(x) - \mathbb{E}[\hat f]) guarantees the attribution is a complete accounting of the specific prediction, an auditor can verify that the stated feature contributions sum exactly to the actual predicted value’s deviation from baseline, so the explanation is the prediction, reconstructed feature by feature, not a plausible-sounding approximation. Consistency guarantees that if the model changes so a feature’s marginal contribution increases, that feature’s Shapley value cannot decrease, which is what makes SHAP values comparable and reproducible across reruns and across similar cases. Together, these mean the organisation can certify that its stated reasons exactly reconstruct the actual decision, and that a regulator or the applicant’s representative who reruns the analysis, or compares it against a similar applicant’s case, gets the same answer, a defensible, reproducible justification.
Grading note: reject an answer that describes local accuracy as merely “SHAP values add up to the prediction” without stating why that matters (auditability/completeness), or that recommends SHAP without naming a specific guarantee.
Model answer (5b): If the organisation used LIME instead, the risk is instability. Consider two nearly identical applicants who differ by a small amount in one continuous variable (e.g., $1 of declared income, or one point of bonus-malus) that happens to sit near a split threshold used repeatedly across the model’s fitted trees, so the model’s local response has a step-like kink between them. LIME explains each point by sampling perturbed points in a neighbourhood defined by a kernel width that must be chosen somewhat arbitrarily, then fitting a linear surrogate to the black box’s behaviour on that sample. Because the sampling is random and the neighbourhood may straddle the kink, two runs on the same instance, or runs on the two nearly-identical applicants, can each land a different local linear fit: one run may identify income as the dominant driver, the neighbouring applicant’s explanation may identify a different variable as dominant, even though the model’s actual output barely changed between the two. A challenger could show that a materially similar applicant received a differently-shaped explanation, which would undermine the credibility of the organisation’s justification and expose it to a claim that its stated reasons for the adverse decision were arbitrary or fabricated after the fact, a real regulatory and litigation risk, not just an inconvenience.
Grading note: the scenario must engage with why LIME is unstable mechanically (kernel width / sampling / local non-smoothness), “LIME is just less reliable” without a mechanism does not meet the bar.

title: INSTRUCTOR SOLUTIONS — Assignment: Explainability Practice
text:
Note



Sample solutions. These are released after marking to help you review your own answers. They illustrate one strong way to answer each question, not the only acceptable one — see each question’s “what a strong answer needs” note for the standard your answer was assessed against.



How to use this guide
This is a hands-on coding assignment on a fixed dataset (Case Study/pg15training.csv) using the lecture’s own fitted frequency model, so — unlike the principles-chapter assignments — there is a genuine right answer for the numerical parts. This guide reports numbers that were actually computed, using the exact frequency-model configuration from the Chapter 5 lecture, reproduced below for reference. Every number below is labelled Verified.
Best boosting iteration 1325, out-of-sample mean Poisson deviance (claim count) 0.48773, observed vs. predicted mean claim frequency 0.16755 vs. 0.16138 — the model is well calibrated at the portfolio level. Your own numbers may differ slightly if you use a different train/test split or refit the model yourself, but the qualitative pattern in each question below should hold. What matters is that your own numbers are internally consistent with your own model, and that your written interpretation is genuinely supported by your own plots and output rather than copied from this guide or the lecture. Question 3 has no fixed numeric answer — it is assessed as a reasoned argument.


Question 1 — PDP and ALE for a new variable
What a strong answer needs: correctly computed PDP and ALE curves for the chosen variable, and a divergence (or agreement) explanation that correctly invokes the correlation structure of the data, not a generic “PDP and ALE are different algorithms.”
Expected, based on the lecture’s own reported findings on this dataset and frequency model, for whichever variable the student selects. For example, if a student selects Density or Value:

A variable moderately correlated with other predictors (e.g. Density, which correlates with several policy/vehicle characteristics) may show a small but visible PDP/ALE divergence in sparse regions of its range (e.g. very high density values), where PDP’s marginalisation is more likely to create unrealistic predictor combinations.
A variable weakly correlated with the rest of the predictor set will tend to show close PDP/ALE agreement, similar to the lecture’s own Age and Bonus findings. The reason is mechanical: PDP’s marginalisation works by holding every other predictor fixed while sweeping the chosen variable, which only creates unrealistic (out-of-distribution) combinations when the chosen variable is correlated with something else. If it isn’t, the combinations PDP averages over are close to combinations that actually occur, so PDP has nothing to correct and lines up with ALE. This is a legitimate and correct finding, not a failure to find divergence.

Grading implication: full credit requires either (i) a correctly identified divergence in a specific region, with a plausible correlation-based explanation naming which other variable(s) the chosen one is correlated with, or (ii) a well-reasoned account of why the divergence is small (i.e., the chosen variable is not strongly correlated with the other predictors, so PDP’s marginalisation assumption is not badly violated) — reasoning (ii) is a legitimate, indeed more accurate, answer for a weakly-correlated variable and should not be marked down relative to a forced “found a big divergence” narrative.
Common mistake to reject: attributing any PDP/ALE gap to “PDP is just less accurate than ALE” without connecting it to the specific correlation between the chosen variable and another predictor, and without identifying where (which region of the variable’s range) the divergence occurs.


Question 2 — SHAP explanations
What a strong answer needs: a correctly computed global SHAP summary with the two most influential features (besides Age and Bonus) correctly identified along with the correct direction of their effect (this is checkable, not a matter of opinion), a genuine individual policy waterfall, and a customer-facing paraphrase in 2c that avoids the jargon the question explicitly flags.

Verified — the two most influential features besides Age and Bonus are Density and Group1.
Verified — direction of effect, checked by correlating each variable’s raw value against its grouped SHAP contribution, and by binning:

Density: higher population density is associated with a higher (more positive) SHAP contribution — i.e. denser areas increase predicted claim frequency, consistent with more traffic and more opportunities for a claim-triggering incident.
Group1: the effect is more mixed across levels, but the highest-numbered Group1 categories tend to carry the largest positive SHAP contributions, suggesting certain vehicle/rating groups within Group1 are associated with materially higher predicted frequency than others.

A student’s own numbers will differ from these (different sample or SHAP run), but a correct SHAP analysis on this dataset should reproduce the qualitative pattern: Bonus and Age dominate, with Density and Group1 as the next tier. Mark down an answer that gets a feature’s direction of effect backwards, or that only restates the ranking without describing direction.
2b/2c — grading note: the waterfall plot for one policy and its accompanying 3–4 sentence explanation should be graded for (i) actually reflecting the SHAP values shown for that specific policy (not a generic restatement of the global pattern), and (ii) genuinely avoiding jargon — reject answers that use “SHAP value,” “marginal contribution,” “baseline,” or similar terms in the customer-facing paragraph. A strong customer-facing answer looks like: “Your predicted claim rate is higher than the average driver’s mainly because of your age and your claims history (bonus-malus level). Being a younger driver is historically associated with a higher chance of a claim, and this pulls your estimate up. [Other factor] pulls it back down somewhat. Together, these are the two biggest reasons your estimate differs from an average policy.” — an answer that gets the direction of an effect backwards while otherwise reading fluently should still be marked down, since a faithful paraphrase requires getting the direction right.


Question 3 — Critically evaluating the toolkit
No fixed numeric answer — grade as a reasoned argument. Part (a) asks for a genuine advantage and a genuine limitation of each of PFI, PDP, ALE, and SHAP; part (b) asks how the methods complement each other for a single adverse decision, not which one method “wins.”
Rubric for 3a — a strong answer names a real, specific advantage and limitation for each method, not a generic restatement of “it has pros and cons.” A model set of four:

PFI: Advantage — cheap, model-agnostic, and captures interaction effects automatically since shuffling a feature disrupts every interaction it participates in; a good first diagnostic. Limitation — as this assignment’s earlier work (or the lecture’s own reporting) shows, it is distorted by correlated and high-cardinality predictors: a high-cardinality variable can rack up large built-in gain importance without being genuinely informative, while permutation importance can understate a variable whose information is redundant with a correlated one.
PDP: Advantage — intuitive and expressed directly on the prediction scale, making it easy to communicate to a non-technical audience (e.g. “predicted frequency rises for younger drivers”). Limitation — assumes feature independence, and can extrapolate into unrealistic predictor combinations when the chosen variable is correlated with others, exactly the failure mode investigated in Question 1.
ALE: Advantage — more robust to correlated predictors than PDP, since it only evaluates the model within locally observed data, avoiding the unrealistic combinations that undermine PDP. Limitation — the resulting values are deviations from the average prediction rather than absolute levels, which is less immediately interpretable to a non-technical audience than a PDP’s direct prediction scale, and it still needs enough observations per bin to be stable.
SHAP: Advantage — the only method with an exact, axiomatically-grounded local decomposition (local accuracy: the attributions sum exactly to the prediction), and it bridges global and local explanation, useful for a single adverse decision specifically. Limitation — computationally heavier than the others for a full dataset, and — as Chapter 4 discusses — a SHAP contribution is an attribution, not a causal claim; it can also mask model bias if the model itself was adversarially constructed (Chapter 4’s discussion of manipulated explanations).

Rubric for 3b — a strong answer:

Recognises that a single adverse decision requires a local explanation, so PFI and PDP/ALE alone cannot serve as the primary account of one applicant’s decision — they describe average portfolio behaviour, not this applicant’s case.
Positions SHAP (the local waterfall) as the natural anchor for explaining this decision, while explaining that PFI and PDP/ALE remain necessary as supporting, population-level context: they let a regulator check the model behaves sensibly and non-discriminatorily on average, and whether this individual’s case looks like an outlier or a typical case — context a single local SHAP value cannot provide on its own.
Does not present any one method as sufficient in isolation — the correct synthesis is that the methods answer different questions (which variables matter overall, how a variable behaves on average, why this specific decision came out this way) and a defensible explanation package needs more than one of them.

Reject: an answer that only ranks the four methods from best to worst without engaging with what each one is actually good and bad at, or that treats any single method as sufficient on its own without acknowledging what it cannot show. Accept equally: different reasonable framings of which specific advantage/limitation pair is most important for each method, provided the stated advantage and limitation are genuine and specific, not generic.

title: INSTRUCTOR SOLUTIONS — Assignment: Privacy Principles
text:
Note



Sample solutions. These are released after marking to help you review your own answers. They illustrate one strong way to answer each question, not the only acceptable one — see each question’s “what a strong answer needs” note for the standard your answer was assessed against.



How to use this guide
Chapter 6’s assignment lets students choose their own domain for most questions rather than mandating insurance. The model answers below use insurance telematics as the illustrative example throughout — for continuity with the lecture’s detailed GM OnStar case study and because it lets each question build on a single running scenario — but any well-reasoned domain (health wearables, workplace monitoring, hiring platforms, smart-home devices) should be graded on the same criteria: correct application of the relevant theoretical framework (Solove, contextual integrity), correct identification of the regulatory principle at stake, and internal consistency with the student’s own chosen scenario. Do not penalise a student for not using insurance.
Two frameworks require precision when grading, since it is easy to approximate them loosely:

Solove’s taxonomy (lecture) has exactly four groups: information collection (surveillance, interrogation), information processing (aggregation, identification, insecurity, secondary use, exclusion), information dissemination (breach of confidentiality, disclosure, exposure, increased accessibility, blackmail, appropriation, distortion), and invasion (intrusion, decisional interference). A student who labels something “aggregation” when it is really “secondary use” (data reused for a different purpose vs. data combined across sources) has made a substantive error, not a stylistic one — check which mechanism actually occurred in their scenario.
Nissenbaum’s contextual integrity (lecture) has five parameters, not four: data subject, sender, recipient, information type, and transmission principle. A common student shortcut is to collapse “information type” into “sender” or omit it — reject answers that only address who-sent/who-received without specifying what kind of information and under what conditions it was appropriate to share.



Question 1 — One scenario, two frameworks
What a strong answer needs: a scenario genuinely distinct from GM OnStar (per the instructions), at least three Solove harms correctly classified against Solove’s actual categories (not invented or approximated ones), all five Nissenbaum parameters correctly identified for the original context (not the secondary use), a mechanistic explanation of why aggregation does not repair a contextual-integrity violation, and a governance control that actually addresses the violated parameter(s) rather than a generic “get more consent.”
Model answer (scenario: a regional auto insurer contracts a third-party telematics vendor, not GM, to run its usage-based insurance app. The vendor’s dongle records trip-level speed, braking, and location data, transmitted to the insurer for pricing):
(a) Scenario: The vendor, separately from its insurer contract, aggregates trip data across all its insurer clients’ customers and sells “driving behaviour segment” profiles to an automotive marketing firm building targeted ad audiences. Customers consented to data collection for their own policy pricing. They were not told the vendor also monetises the aggregated data this way.
(b) Applying Solove’s taxonomy, three harms:








Harm
Solove category
Why




Continuous recording of every trip, including location, regardless of relevance to a pricing decision
Surveillance (information collection)
The vendor watches and records more behaviour than any single pricing decision requires


Combining trip-level speed/braking/location data across the customer base into marketable “segments”
Aggregation (information processing)
Individually innocuous trip records become a revealing behavioural profile once combined


Selling that profile to a marketing firm for ad targeting, a purpose the customer never agreed to
Secondary use (information processing)
Data collected for pricing is repurposed for marketing without new consent



Grading note — acceptable alternatives: “Breach of confidentiality” is also defensible for the sale itself if the student argues the vendor contract with the insurer implied non-disclosure to third parties. “Exclusion” is defensible if the scenario includes customers being unable to find out that their data was sold. Reject “surveillance” applied to the sale (surveillance is about collection, not downstream use) and reject any harm invented outside the four Solove groups (e.g., a student writing “commercialisation” as if it were a Solove category).
(c) Applying Nissenbaum’s contextual integrity to the same scenario, norms of the original context:







Parameter
Original context




Data subject
The customer


Sender
The customer (via the vendor’s dongle, opted into for the insurer’s pricing programme)


Recipient
The vendor and the insurer, for pricing the customer’s own policy


Information type
Individual trip-level driving-behaviour data (speed, braking, location, time of day)


Transmission principle
Shared under the UBI programme’s terms, for pricing the sender’s own policy, not for resale or third-party use



Aggregating the data changes whether an individual record can be extracted from the release, but it does not change who receives the data or under what conditions it was originally shared, and those are two of the five parameters that define whether a flow is appropriate. The marketing firm is not the recipient the customer had in mind when they opted into the programme, and “for our own pricing” is not the same transmission principle as “resold to any interested third party.” Contextual integrity is violated the moment the recipient or transmission principle changes, independent of whether the released file is aggregated or individually identifiable. This is precisely why the lecture insists contextual integrity is not about secrecy. A dataset can be perfectly non-identifiable and still constitute a privacy violation if it flows to the wrong recipient or under the wrong principle.
Grading note: reject answers that argue aggregation “solves” the contextual integrity problem, or that treat re-identifiability as the only thing that matters. That conflates contextual integrity with mere anonymisation, which is the opposite of the lecture’s point.
(d) Model answer: A defensible control is a purpose-specific secondary-use authorisation. Before any aggregated data leaves the organisation for a use beyond the original transmission principle, require (i) a data-sharing agreement that names the recipient and the specific permitted purpose, (ii) a renewed, specific disclosure to customers (not buried in the original UBI terms) describing this new flow, with an opt-out or opt-in mechanism, and (iii) sign-off that the new use is consistent with the purpose-limitation principle (GDPR Art 5 / APP 6) rather than merely “not individually identifiable.” This effectively re-establishes appropriate norms for a new, disclosed context rather than silently repurposing the original one. Reject “just anonymise it better” or “add more noise” as a sufficient answer on its own. Those address re-identification risk, not the contextual integrity violation identified in (c), which is about recipient and transmission principle, not data granularity. A technical PET can be part of the answer but must be paired with the governance/consent element to actually address the norm violation.


Question 2 — Choosing a privacy-enhancing technique
What a strong answer needs: a technique recommendation for each scenario that is justified by the actual utility-privacy trade-off for that scenario’s threat model and data-granularity need — not a reflexive “always use k-anonymity” or “always use the strongest PET available.” The most common error is recommending a PET for scenario (a) at all; internal full-dataset access typically calls for governance controls, not data transformation. Scenario (d) tests something different: recognising that federated learning solves a problem the other three techniques cannot, because it is the only one of the four that avoids centralising data at all rather than transforming a dataset before or after release.
Model answer (insurance domain; the same reasoning transfers to any domain the student chose):
(a) Internal analytics team needs the full individual-level dataset to build a new model.
Recommendation: no PET — strict access control and governance instead (pseudonymisation of direct identifiers at most). The team needs individual-level granularity to fit a model at all; applying k-anonymity, DP noise, or synthetic generation here would degrade the very data the model needs, for a threat that isn’t present — the “attacker” in this scenario is an authorised internal employee, not an external party receiving a release. The correct control for this stage is organisational: role-based access, logging, a documented legal basis and purpose limitation, and (if direct identifiers such as policy number or name are present) pseudonymisation so identifiers are separated from the analytics dataset. Grading note: a student who recommends k-anonymity or DP for this scenario has misapplied the technique — PETs are for releasing or sharing data outside its original custody boundary, not for controlling access within it. This is the one answer in this question with a clearly wrong “obvious” choice that the question is specifically testing for.
(b) A business partner (reinsurer, benefits administrator, recruitment agency) needs portfolio- or cohort-level data, not individual records.
Recommendation: k-anonymity (or straightforward aggregation to cohort level). The partner’s stated need is already at the cohort level, so generalising quasi-identifiers (age bands, region bands) until every group has at least k members matches the actual use case with minimal utility loss — the partner never needed individual rows, so suppressing/generalising down to groups of size k costs little relative to what they asked for. This also produces a dataset whose record structure survives (still one row per group, interpretable for portfolio analysis), unlike DP noise or synthetic records, which the partner may not need and which would complicate their own downstream reporting for no additional privacy benefit given the already-aggregated use case.
(c) Public release to support academic research.
Recommendation: synthetic data, or differential privacy if only specific published statistics (not a full dataset) are needed. A public release faces an unbounded, unknown adversary with no data-sharing agreement to constrain reuse — this is exactly the setting that calls for a formal, released-artefact guarantee rather than a governance promise. Synthetic data (ideally generated with a differentially private training step) lets external researchers work with realistic record-level data and fit their own models, which cohort-level k-anonymised data cannot support. If the goal is narrower — releasing a specific set of published statistics rather than a usable dataset — differential privacy applied directly to those statistics is the tighter, more auditable choice, since it comes with a provable bound on any single record’s influence on the release, which matters when the recipient population and their intentions cannot be controlled or vetted.
Grading note: accept differential privacy over synthetic data for (c) if the student’s justification correctly distinguishes “releasing a dataset for modelling” (favours synthetic data) from “releasing specific statistics” (favours DP directly) — both are defensible provided the reasoning engages with what the recipients actually need to do with the release. Reject any answer for (c) that recommends k-anonymity alone with no further guarantee — the lecture’s own comparison table is explicit that k-anonymity gives no probabilistic guarantee and is vulnerable to background-knowledge attacks, which is precisely the situation of an unknown public audience.
(d) Several organisations want to jointly train a shared model, but none will send raw data to the others or a third party.
Recommendation: federated learning. This is the one scenario where none of the first three techniques actually fits. k-anonymity and synthetic data both require someone to hold and transform a dataset before releasing it, and differential privacy still requires a party willing to compute on and publish a statistic from pooled data. Here, by construction, no party is willing to centralise the data at all, even briefly. Federated learning solves the actual problem: each organisation trains the shared model locally on its own data and sends back only the model’s updated parameters, never a record, to be aggregated. This is the same setup WeBank’s FATE platform supports for credit scoring across Chinese financial institutions.
Grading note: reject an answer that reaches for k-anonymity, DP, or synthetic data here, unless the student explicitly argues each organisation would first need to release a transformed dataset to a shared location, which reintroduces exactly the centralisation problem the scenario rules out. Accept “federated learning, though the technique remains mostly at pilot stage for this kind of cross-institution use case” as a defensible caveat, matching the lecture’s own honesty about the state of adoption outside banking. Also accept an answer noting that federated learning alone does not guarantee privacy of the model updates themselves, and recommends pairing it with differential privacy or secure aggregation, if the student engages with this nuance from the lecture rather than treating federated learning as automatically private.


Question 3 — Data Protection Impact Assessment
What a strong answer needs: headings that plausibly walk through the OAIC’s four-step DPIA process (identify, assess, recommend, respond) and privacy-by-design considerations, applied to a continuous-behavioural-data product — not a generic “privacy policy” outline copied from elsewhere.
Model answer (8–10 sections is typical; reasonable variation is fine):







Section
What it covers




Purpose and scope of the product
What the app/device does, what decision the collected data supports, and who is affected


Data flow mapping
What is collected, from whom, how often, and who (internal teams, vendors, third parties) has access at each stage


Legal basis and consent mechanism
The lawful basis for collection and how consent (or another basis) is obtained and recorded


Data minimisation review
Whether each collected field is necessary for the stated purpose, or should be dropped/aggregated


Sensitive and derived data assessment
Whether any collected or inferable data (location, health-adjacent inferences) falls into a sensitive category requiring extra protection


Risk assessment against regulatory obligations
Privacy risks identified against GDPR Art 5 / APP obligations, and against community expectations (does the actual use match what a reasonable data subject would expect?)


Re-identification and third-party risk
Quasi-identifier and aggregation risk if any data is shared externally, including with data brokers or platform partners


Recommended controls
Proposed technical (encryption, access control, PET selection) and organisational (contracts, retention limits) mitigations


Residual risk and accountability
Documented residual risk after controls, and the named owner accountable for the decision to proceed


Review schedule
When the DPIA will be revisited (e.g. on any material change to data flows or vendors)



Grading note: the “data flow mapping” and “third-party risk” sections are the two most important to see given the chapter’s own emphasis on connected devices and OEM-style data pipelines — a DPIA for a continuous-behavioural-data product that doesn’t explicitly ask “who besides us receives this data” has missed the chapter’s central lesson (the GM OnStar case turned entirely on an unexamined third-party data flow). Accept a shorter list (6–7 sections) if it still covers identify/assess/recommend/respond and explicitly addresses third-party data sharing; reject a list that only covers internal security controls with no treatment of consent, purpose limitation, or downstream data flows.

title: INSTRUCTOR SOLUTIONS — Assignment: Privacy Practice
text:
Note



Sample solutions. These are released after marking to help you review your own answers. They illustrate one strong way to answer each question, not the only acceptable one — see each question’s “what a strong answer needs” note for the standard your answer was assessed against.



How to use this guide
This is a fixed-dataset, fixed-tooling coding assignment (pg15training, sdcMicro, synthpop) that reuses objects the Chapter 7 lecture already builds (df_raw, df_sdc, sdc, df_synth_input, syn_df, df_real_holdout, model_real, model_syn). Every number below was produced by actually running the lecture’s own code end to end (R 4.3, sdcMicro, synthpop, tidyverse, seed 42, in the same order the lecture executes it), then appending exactly the code each question asks for. No number here is estimated or reconstructed from the lecture text.
What is and isn’t reproducible exactly. createSdcObj(), localSuppression(), and syn() are deterministic given the same seed and the same sequence of prior random draws, so if you (or a student) run the lecture’s code and then this guide’s code in the same session, in the same order, you should get the same numbers reported here to the precision shown. The DP sections (Question 2) call runif() fresh for every draw, so any single DP estimate will differ run to run, including between students, even with the same seed, once other random draws happen at different points in their script. What should not differ is the pattern: which subgroup shows more noise, and whether that noise roughly tracks the sensitivity formula.


Question 1 — Re-identification risk and k-anonymity with AgeGroup removed
What a strong answer needs: a correct createSdcObj() call with the specified four-variable keyVars, correctly reported risk numbers, a correct localSuppression() call at k=20 with the right importance vector, and reasoning in (b) and (d) that engages with the actual numbers rather than restating “fewer quasi-identifiers is safer” in the abstract.
Code — part (a):
sdc_noage <- createSdcObj(
  dat     = df_sdc,
  keyVars = c("Gender", "DensityGroup", "ValueGroup", "BonusGroup"),
  numVars = c("ClaimAmount")
)
sdc_noage@risk$global$risk_pct
sum(sdc_noage@risk$individual[, 2] <= 5)

(b) — model answer. Removing AgeGroup decreases global risk by about six-fold, from 0.77% to 0.13%, and eliminates the small-group problem entirely: no record has an equivalence class of 5 or fewer once AgeGroup is dropped (versus 102 records in the lecture’s five-variable set). This is the size of change you would expect from removing “one of the most identifying variables”: every quasi-identifier narrows the equivalence classes that share a record’s value, and AgeGroup was doing more of that narrowing than any of the other four. Removing a quasi-identifier can only ever coarsen equivalence classes (merge groups, never split them further), so risk falling, not rising, is the only possible direction; the question is how much, and here the answer is “most of it” — AgeGroup alone accounts for roughly 83% of the five-variable risk.
Code — part (c):
sdc_noage_k100 <- localSuppression(sdc_noage, k = 100, importance = c(1, 2, 3, 4))
sdc_noage_k100@risk$global$risk_pct

Global risk after k=100: 0.12% (down from 0.13% before suppression).
(d) — model answer. At k = 100 on this four-variable set, localSuppression() suppresses 682 values, all in BonusGroup, moving global risk only slightly (0.13% \to 0.12%). The suppression is even more concentrated than the lecture’s k = 50, five-variable result: there, suppression eventually spilled over into a second variable (ValueGroup, 0.44%) once BonusGroup alone could no longer close every group; here, BonusGroup alone is still enough at k=100. Directly counting the four-variable groups (df_sdc %>% count(Gender, DensityGroup, ValueGroup, BonusGroup)) shows why: the four quasi-identifiers combine into only 2 \times 4 \times 4 \times 4 = 128 possible groups, and the smallest already contains 66 records. Since 66 < 100, some suppression is now required (unlike at k=20, where the smallest group already cleared the bar and nothing was suppressed at all), but because every group is already fairly close to size 100, only a modest, single-variable fix is needed to bring the shortfall groups up to threshold. Removing AgeGroup beforehand changes the comparison in two ways at once: it starts the four-variable set from much lower risk (0.13% vs. 0.77%), and it makes the remaining variables coarse enough, in combination, that a much higher k is needed before suppression becomes as extensive as the lecture’s five-variable, k=50 result.
Grading note: do not penalise a student whose 4-variable global risk or suppression numbers differ slightly from the table above if their code is correct — small differences can arise if their df_sdc/sdc objects were built from a different-order pipeline. What must be correct is the direction and rough size of the changes: risk should drop substantially (not stay flat, not rise) when AgeGroup is removed, and suppression at k=100 on the reduced set should be modest and concentrated in BonusGroup, not comparable in scale to the lecture’s k=50, five-variable result. An answer that reports suppression spread across multiple variables at k=100 on this four-variable set, or that finds global risk barely changes when AgeGroup is dropped, has a coding error worth checking (most likely: AgeGroup was not actually removed from keyVars, or importance has the wrong length).


Question 2 — Differential privacy for policyholders aged 66+ in dense urban areas
What a strong answer needs: a correct dp_mean sweep on the specified subgroup across all five epsilon values, a genuine report of the subgroup’s size and noise pattern, and a quantitative (not just directional) comparison of the observed noise to the sensitivity formula and to the lecture’s two benchmark groups.
Code — part (a)/(b):
sub_grp <- df_raw %>% filter(AgeGroup == "66+", DensityGroup == "Dense urban")
nrow(sub_grp)               # subgroup size n
mean(sub_grp$Age)           # true mean age

results_sub <- map_dfr(epsilons, function(eps) {
  tibble(epsilon = eps,
         `DP mean age` = round(dp_mean(sub_grp$Age, lower = 18, upper = 100, epsilon = eps), 2))
})

(Sensitivity for this subgroup: (100-18)/1{,}490 = 0.0550. Theoretical Laplace SD = \sqrt{2} \times \text{sensitivity} / \varepsilon.)
(c) — model answer. The empirical spread of the 200 draws tracks the theoretical Laplace SD closely at every epsilon (e.g. 0.722 observed vs. 0.778 predicted at \varepsilon=0.1; 0.073 vs. 0.078 at \varepsilon=1), confirming the sensitivity formula. More importantly, this subgroup (n=1{,}490) sits, exactly as the sensitivity formula predicts, between the lecture’s two benchmarks: its sensitivity (0.0550) is about 67 times larger than the whole portfolio’s (0.00082, n=100{,}000), since 100{,}000/1{,}490 \approx 67, and about 3 times smaller than the rare subgroup’s (0.168, n=487), since 1{,}490/487 \approx 3.06, matching the sensitivity ratio 0.168/0.0550 \approx 3.06 almost exactly. In practical terms: at \varepsilon=0.1, this subgroup’s noise (multi-tenths of a year, occasionally over a year) is far larger than the whole portfolio’s (a fraction of a day) but noticeably smaller than the n=487 rare group’s (multiple years). This is the sensitivity formula working exactly as advertised: noise scales with 1/n, so a subgroup’s size, not just the chosen \varepsilon, determines how much accuracy a DP release costs.
Grading note: because DP draws are stochastic, do not expect a student’s single-draw table to match the table above exactly, or even to be centred as tightly — accept any answer whose pattern is right: noise shrinking as \varepsilon grows, and this subgroup’s noise magnitude sitting visibly between the lecture’s whole-portfolio and rare-subgroup results (not comparable to either extreme). A student who ran only one draw per epsilon (permitted by the question, since only “the same dp_mean sweep” is required) may report noisier-looking numbers than the 200-draw averages here; that is expected and should not be penalised provided their qualitative comparison to the two benchmarks is sound. Reject an answer that reports noise at \varepsilon=0.1 comparable to the whole-portfolio benchmark (near-zero) or comparable to the rare-subgroup benchmark (multi-year) — a subgroup with n=1{,}490 should visibly not match either extreme.


Question 3 — Synthetic data: TSTR for predicting Gender
What a strong answer needs: a correctly specified logistic regression predicting Gender, fitted separately on df_synth_input and syn_df, correctly evaluated via auc_manual() on df_real_holdout, and a genuine, numerically grounded explanation in (c) rather than a generic restatement of “synthetic data loses some fidelity.”
Code:
fit_gender_model <- function(df) {
  glm(I(Gender == "Male") ~ Age + log1p(Density) + log1p(Value) + Bonus,
      family = binomial(link = "logit"), data = df)
}
gmodel_real <- fit_gender_model(df_synth_input)
gmodel_syn  <- fit_gender_model(syn_df)

holdout_gender_actual <- as.integer(df_real_holdout$Gender == "Male")
pred_g_real <- predict(gmodel_real, newdata = df_real_holdout, type = "response")
pred_g_syn  <- predict(gmodel_syn,  newdata = df_real_holdout, type = "response")

auc_manual(pred_g_real, holdout_gender_actual)
auc_manual(pred_g_syn,  holdout_gender_actual)

−0.006
